A-01e1.text: FMs predict protein structures, mutation effects, and cellular responses to genetic perturbations.

1-02e1.text: FMs: general patterns extracted once at development, then applied to many problems (ESM2, Geneformer, Evo 2...).

1-10e2.text: Scope of the review: molecular sequences, macromolecular structures, single-cell data, and other omics; the concepts likely apply more broadly in biology and medicine.

2.1-01e3.text: Task-specific models also covered because they rest on the same premise and are frequently used as FMs: AlphaFold (structure), AlphaGenome (sequence-to-function), virtual cells (perturbation).

1-02e2.text: Agents: biologists with limited programming experience can apply advanced computational tools to their own datasets.

1-05e1.text: Recognized successes are in conventional bioinformatics and biostatistics (GeneAgent, CellVoyager, TxAgent).

1-05e2.text: Independent benchmarks (BixBench, HeurekaBench) show agents remain brittle on realistic analysis tasks.

1-06e1.text: AlphaFold + Biomni: both draw on public resources (UniProt, PDB). AlphaFold can predict an uncharacterized protein's structure, which an agent composing existing software cannot do; the multistep work after that (compare with known structures, link to variants/expression data, plan follow-up experiments) is what an agent can assemble.

3-01e1.text: Typical task: "which genes respond to a drug in this single-cell dataset?" → plan the analysis, write and run code, call an FM, check results, return to the user when a decision is needed.

3-04e1.text: Biomni: composes workflows from tools and protocols mined from thousands of publications. Paper2Agent: turns a paper's codebase into MCP tools.

3-04e2.text: Other agents target chemistry, gene-set annotation, gene editing, single-cell reanalysis, therapeutics.

5.1-03e2.text: Evidence on adoption by biologists remains limited to surveys.

6.1-02e1.text: Route each question to the model whose boundary covers it; combine outputs from complementary models; fall back to a simple baseline when no model applies.

6.2-01e2.text: Recent high-profile agent studies still rely on human scientists to run experiments and interpret results.

3-07e2.text: Unlike conventional bioinformatics tools, FMs have little community guidance on when to trust them.

3-07e3.text: At an LDL cholesterol locus, the AlphaGenome agent prioritized SORT1, whereas the original paper emphasized CELSR2 and PSRC1.

6.1-01e1.text: GPN-MSA (evolutionary alignments) and ChromBPNet (single assay at base resolution) already follow this pattern.

1-01e1.text: Processing: Fourier calculations turned X-ray diffraction data into the first protein structure (myoglobin).

1-01e2.text: Interpreting: the Protein Data Bank grew from 7 structures (1971) to 250,000+, driving new methods for comparing and classifying structures; new disciplines formed (biostatistics, bioinformatics, computational biology).

1-01e3.text: Discovering: AlphaFold predicts protein structure from sequence, producing results not yet tested experimentally.

1-04e3.text: Crude-oil analogy (Fig 1C): raw data are refined into a reusable intermediate and distributed to diverse downstream users.

2.1.1-05e1.text: Individual numbers may combine properties; a human could not identify which number reflects, say, polarity.

2.1.1-05e3.text: In ESM2, proteins with similar structure or function lie near one another in embedding space even when their sequences differ.

1-04e1.text: ESM2 is trained on UniRef sequences; Nucleotide Transformer and Evo 2 learn from genomes across species; Geneformer, scGPT, UCE learn from tens of millions of cells.

1-04e2.text: AlphaFold predicts structure accurately without "learning" the physical and chemical basis of folding (Fig 1B).

4.2-01e2.text: Not captured: a protein language model predicting residue contacts has no representation of the forces driving folding.

4.3-04e1.text: Enformer predicts regulatory signals across the genome well but poorly explains differences in expression between individuals and often predicts the wrong direction of effect; a 2026 preprint reports the same for AlphaGenome and Borzoi.
4.3-04e1.finding: Observed states rarely predict the effect of an intervention beyond simple baselines

4.3-04e5.text: Masked and autoregressive objectives reward predicting what occurs together, not what causes what.
4.3-04e5.finding: Observed states rarely predict the effect of an intervention beyond simple baselines

3-01e2.text: Starting point, the limits of chat LLMs (widely available from late 2022): knowledge fixed at a training cutoff, no source for answers, hallucinations, cannot act on data or run software.

2.1-01e1.text: Masking example: hide a few amino acids → model predicts them → compare with the truth → adjust → repeat across millions of sequences.

2.1-01e2.text: Why it suits biology: hundreds of millions of unlabeled DNA/protein sequences and single-cell transcriptomes vs. scarce, labor-intensive, unevenly distributed validated labels (e.g., a variant classified pathogenic or benign).

2.1-02e1.text: Patterns the training is designed to extract: pairs of amino acids that mutate together because they contact each other in the fold; TF-bound short motifs in DNA (e.g., the TATA box in many promoters); groups of genes whose expression rises and falls together in a pathway.

4.2-01e1.text: Captured: amino acid chemistry, which residues contact each other in a fold, which mutations a protein tolerates.

4.2-02e1.text: Protein language models are never told amino acid properties, yet embeddings group residues by hydrophobicity and charge.
4.2-02e1.finding: Known patterns can be recovered from unlabeled sequence

4.2-02e2.text: They recover which residues physically interact in the fold, because such residues tend to mutate together over evolution.
4.2-02e2.finding: Known patterns can be recovered from unlabeled sequence

4.2-02e3.text: ESMFold predicts atomic-level structure from a single sequence; AlphaFold, which also uses alignments of related sequences, reached near-experimental accuracy in blind CASP14.
4.2-02e3.finding: Known patterns can be recovered from unlabeled sequence

4.3-07e1.text: Fine-tuning can add knowledge from the new labels, so a strong fine-tuned score does not show how much was learned in pretraining.
4.3-07e1.finding: A correct answer does not show the model knows why

2.1-02e2.text: Zero-shot example: a protein language model scores how plausible a sequence is; a mutation that makes it much less plausible is more likely to disrupt function, so the score estimates variant effect.

4.2-03e1.text: Protein language model likelihoods predict mutational effects without mutational training data and correlate with deep mutational scanning measurements.

4.2-03e2.text: EVE (unsupervised model of evolutionary variation) matched or exceeded supervised methods at classifying human variants as pathogenic or benign.

4.2-03e3.text: ProteinGym turned this into a shared test of more than 200 deep mutational scanning assays.

4.2-06e3.text: General protein language models guided antibody evolution toward improved binding without task-specific training.
4.2-06e3.finding: Learned knowledge can be read out

2.1.1-02e2.text: ESM2: the 20 standard amino acids are the vocabulary, so a 300-aa protein is 300 tokens.

2.2.1-04e3.text: Fixed gene identities from specific genome annotations restrict models to species seen in training; UCE addresses this.
2.2.1-04e3.finding: Single-cell: representing expression levels; fixed gene vocabulary

2.1.1-02e1.text: LLMs: tokens = words or word fragments. Biological FMs: tokens = amino acids, nucleotides, or short motifs; in single-cell models, genes (each cell read as a list of the genes it expresses).

2.1.1-02e3.text: DNA: model builders must choose among single nucleotides, fixed-length *k*-mers, or learned multi-nucleotide tokens.

2.2.1-02e1.text: Nucleotide Transformer: fixed six-nucleotide *k*-mers. DNABERT-2 and GROVER: learned variable-length tokens.
2.2.1-02e1.finding: DNA: how to define a token

2.2.1-02e2.text: Multinucleotide tokens can split regulatory motifs and hide the effect of a single-nucleotide variant.
2.2.1-02e2.finding: DNA: how to define a token

2.2.1-02e3.text: HyenaDNA, Caduceus, Evo: one nucleotide per token, with architectures efficient over long inputs.
2.2.1-02e3.finding: DNA: how to define a token

2.2.1-04e1.text: Why hard: a cell has no inherent order, each gene carries a continuous value, and platform/processing details create strong non-biological confounders.
2.2.1-04e1.finding: Single-cell: representing expression levels; fixed gene vocabulary

2.2.1-04e2.text: Geneformer: genes ordered by expression rank. scGPT: each gene paired with a binned expression value.
2.2.1-04e2.finding: Single-cell: representing expression levels; fixed gene vocabulary

4.1-02e2.text: Tokenization fixes the smallest unit: a six-nucleotide token blurs a single-nucleotide variant; a rank-based input discards how strongly each gene is expressed.
4.1-02e2.finding: Single-cell: representing expression levels; fixed gene vocabulary

2.1.1-03e1.text: Proteins: rules dictated by evolution; a gene persists only if the protein folds into the required structure and adopts the right dynamics.

2.1.1-03e2.text: Regulatory DNA: the grammar lies in the number, spacing, orientation, and order of motifs, determining which TFs bind together, how strongly the gene is expressed, and in which cell types.

2.2.1-04e4.text: Single-cell models: the grammar is co-expression patterns, the token is a gene, and the corpus is a matrix of expression counts across cells.
2.2.1-04e4.finding: Single-cell: representing expression levels; fixed gene vocabulary

2.1.1-04e1.text: Examples: UniRef (hundreds of millions of protein sequences; trained ESM2); CZ CELLxGENE Discover (150M+ single cells; supplied scGPT's training data).

2.1.1-04e2.text: Size: ESM3 (~771B tokens) vs. Llama 3 (~15T tokens), roughly 20-fold fewer, though tokens from the two domains are not directly equivalent.

2.1.1-04e3.text: Diversity: many sequences are near-duplicates of close relatives (hence clustering before training); sequences concentrate in a few well-studied lineages, biasing model likelihoods toward them.

2.1.1-04e4.text: Nature of the data: text records language directly; biological data are indirect measurements shaped by assay technology and experimental design, containing only what current methods can measure and what researchers chose to study.

4.1-02e1.text: Human proteins and model organisms are represented by many related sequences and measured cell states; poorly studied lineages and rarely profiled cell states appear seldom or not at all.

4.3-02e3.text: Spatial, perturbation, and bulk corpora are small compared with sequence databases and single-cell atlases; more parameters cannot recover patterns the data never contain.
4.3-02e3.finding: Models capture both biology and the history of sampling

5.2-03e2.text: Unlike text, biology's corpus is still being defined as new measurement technologies emerge.
5.2-03e2.finding: Models capture both biology and the history of sampling

2.1.1-05e2.text: The "Jennifer Aniston neuron" in neuroscience (a single neuron firing selectively to one person) motivates the sparse-autoencoder aim.

4.2-06e1.text: Sparse autoencoders have recovered features for active sites, zinc-finger domains, and disulfide bonds in protein language models.
4.2-06e1.finding: Learned knowledge can be read out

2.1.2-02e1.text: ESM2: UniRef sequences, tokenized as individual amino acids. Geneformer: each cell as a list of genes ranked by expression.

2.1.2-01e1.text: ESM2 can score a mutation absent from its training data, but cannot score nucleotide substitutions because its vocabulary contains only amino acids.

4.1-05e1.text: A model tested only on data resembling its training set can look strong while failing on new proteins, species, or conditions.

4.1-05e2.text: If test proteins have close relatives in the training set, a high score may reflect recall rather than learned rules.

4.2-05e1.text: SaProt pairs each amino acid with a token for its local structure.
4.2-05e1.finding: Generalization improves by enriching what each token encodes, not by adding parameters

4.2-05e2.text: GPN-MSA adds aligned sequences from 100 vertebrate genomes, making conservation visible, and outperforms sequence-only models at predicting deleterious variants.
4.2-05e2.finding: Generalization improves by enriching what each token encodes, not by adding parameters

4.2-05e3.text: UCE represents each gene by the ESM2 embedding of its protein, so it can place cells from species absent from training in a shared space.
4.2-05e3.finding: Generalization improves by enriching what each token encodes, not by adding parameters

4.3-03e1.text: AlphaFold2 relies heavily on related sequences and largely fails to predict the structural disruption of destabilizing point mutations.
4.3-03e1.finding: One-mutation effects are often missed, and scale has not closed the gap

4.3-03e3.text: AlphaGenome reads one megabase at a time (underlying its state-of-the-art performance), yet longer-range or inter-chromosomal regulation lies outside a single input.
4.3-03e3.finding: One-mutation effects are often missed, and scale has not closed the gap

2.1.2-03e1.text: Alternatives built on features of the data: HyenaDNA (long genomic context), Caduceus (equivalence of the two DNA strands), PINNACLE (protein interaction networks).

4.1-04e1.text: ESM2 likelihoods score tolerance of a mutation but ESM2 is not built to write new sequences; ProGen2 and Evo are natural generators of new proteins and genomes.

4.2-04e1.text: ProGen produced artificial lysozymes with measurable catalytic activity.
4.2-04e1.finding: Models can design new, functional molecules

4.2-04e2.text: ESM3, prompted with structure and function tokens, generated a fluorescent protein distant from known natural sequences.
4.2-04e2.finding: Models can design new, functional molecules

2.1.2-04e2.text: Contrastive: Orthrus (splice isoforms and orthologs of the same gene as related RNAs); SCimilarity (cells of the same type placed near one another).

4.1-04e2.text: SCimilarity's embeddings suit searching an atlas for similar cells, not predicting perturbation response.

2.1.2-05e1.text: Intrinsic: ESM2 recovering residue contacts. Downstream: predicting mutation effects on ProteinGym.

5.1-02e1.text: Bulk transcriptomics has no dedicated FM benchmark; spatial benchmarks are only emerging; multi-omics and RNA models have few head-to-head comparisons.

5.1-02e2.text: Protein structure (CASP), protein fitness (ProteinGym), and perturbation prediction (Virtual Cell Challenge) have blind or community-maintained evaluations; sequence-to-function models are mostly evaluated on developer-defined suites, with cross-individual tests appearing only recently.

2.1.2-06e1.text: Using a model as is: scoring mutations by likelihood; Geneformer's *in silico* deletion.

4.2-06e2.text: Geneformer's simulated gene deletion nominated therapeutic targets for cardiomyopathy that were then supported experimentally.
4.2-06e2.finding: Learned knowledge can be read out

2.1.2-06e2.text: Interpretability: which input positions drive a prediction; which internal features match known biology.

4.1-06e1.text: Probing, fine-tuning, and interpretability analysis each expose different knowledge.

4.3-07e2.text: Attention weights should not be read as biological mechanisms; sparse-autoencoder dictionaries so far cover only a few protein and genomic models.
4.3-07e2.finding: A correct answer does not show the model knows why

4.3-07e3.text: For most models it remains unknown whether a correct prediction reflects real biology or a shortcut that works on the test.
4.3-07e3.finding: A correct answer does not show the model knows why

2.2.1-03e1.text: Single-stranded RNA folds back on itself; RNA-FM and RiNALMo (trained on tens of millions of non-coding RNAs) recover which bases pair, much as ESM2 recovers protein contacts.
2.2.1-03e1.finding: RNA: models read sequence and fold structure; non-coding RNA models need not capture mRNA function

2.2.1-03e2.text: mRNA: function depends on coding sequence, splicing, regulatory regions; Orthrus uses contrastive learning across splice isoforms and orthologs.
2.2.1-03e2.finding: RNA: models read sequence and fold structure; non-coding RNA models need not capture mRNA function

2.2.1-06e1.text: ESM2 and ProtTrans established how much can be learned from sequence alone at scale.
2.2.1-06e1.finding: Protein: the vocabulary is settled, so innovation moves to other design elements

2.2.1-06e2.text: SaProt and ESM3 add structure/function tokens; ProGen2 adopts next-token prediction for generation; Ankh matches larger models at a fraction of the pretraining cost.
2.2.1-06e2.finding: Protein: the vocabulary is settled, so innovation moves to other design elements

2.2.1-07e1.text: GeneCompass: enriches gene tokens with prior knowledge.
2.2.1-07e1.finding: Multi-omics: no shared vocabulary; models take different routes to align modalities

2.2.1-07e3.text: AIDO: separate DNA, RNA, protein, and cell models, with embeddings combined.
2.2.1-07e3.finding: Multi-omics: no shared vocabulary; models take different routes to align modalities

2.2-01e1.text: Contrast: a general-purpose LLM serves many kinds of text and tasks.
2.2-01e1.finding: Multi-omics: no shared vocabulary; models take different routes to align modalities

2.2.1-05e1.text: BulkFormer: trained on bulk profiles linked to tissue type, disease, and clinical outcome; gene remains the vocabulary unit.
2.2.1-05e1.finding: Bulk and spatial: bulk trades resolution for clinical linkage; spatial adds neighborhood

2.2.1-05e2.text: Nicheformer: trained jointly on dissociated and spatial data, so a cell's embedding reflects its expression and its neighborhood. VirTues: extends spatial modeling to protein markers in multiplexed tissue images.
2.2.1-05e2.finding: Bulk and spatial: bulk trades resolution for clinical linkage; spatial adds neighborhood

2.2.1-07e2.text: PINNACLE: protein interaction networks built per cell type; the same protein gets a different embedding in each cell type.
2.2.1-07e2.finding: Multi-omics: no shared vocabulary; models take different routes to align modalities

2.2.2-02e1.text: ESM2 embeddings used to predict structure, annotate function, and score mutations.

2.2.2-02e2.text: What is embedded: a residue or protein (ESM2), a DNA segment (Nucleotide Transformer, Evo), a gene in context (Geneformer, scGPT), a whole cell (UCE).

2.2.2-03e1.text: AlphaFold: amino acid sequence → 3D coordinates of every atom (from PDB structures).

2.2.2-03e2.text: AlphaGenome: up to 1 Mb of sequence → thousands of tracks (RNA expression, chromatin accessibility, TF binding) at up to single-base resolution; extends Enformer and Borzoi; Scooby adapts Borzoi to single cells.

2.2.2-03e3.text: Variant-effect predictors (clinical labels are scarce, so they use other signals): EVE (evolutionary conservation), AlphaMissense (adapts AlphaFold with human population frequencies), popEVE (combines both so scores are comparable across proteins).

4.3-06e1.text: AlphaMissense: meaningful discordance with curated clinical evidence across 5,845 missense variants in 59 disease genes.

4.3-06e2.text: Structure-confidence scores poorly separated successes from failures among 614 experimentally characterized de novo protein designs.

2.2.2-04e1.text: Proteins: ProGen (protein-family tag → full sequence, one amino acid at a time); ESM3 (prompted with partial structure or function).

2.2.2-04e2.text: Nucleic acids: Evo (genomes), regLM (regulatory DNA with specified activity), CodonTransformer (organism-specific codons), gRNAde (RNA that folds into a target structure).

2.2.2-04e3.text: Perturbation: CellOT (maps control onto perturbed populations), GEARS (gene-relationship graph for unseen combinations), State (trained on a large perturbation corpus, treats whole cells as tokens).

3-02e1.text: External components that can extend the system: documents, tools, or a connected FM.

3-07e1.text: A reasoning model's written steps are not guaranteed valid or faithful; biological inference, unlike mathematical proof, starts from incomplete premises that only experiments can test.

3-03e1.text: MCP analogy: like USB for computer devices; a database, program, or FM wrapped once as an MCP tool can be used by any compatible agent.

3-03e2.text: Skill file contents: steps of a standard analysis, or when a tool's output should not be trusted.

3-04e3.text: Virtual Lab: agents acting as a principal investigator and specialist scientists designed nanobodies; the AI co-scientist and Robin extend this to hypothesis generation.

1-06e2.text: Agents calling FMs as tools: Biomni, Virtual Biotech.

3-05e1.text: Tool: Virtual Lab agents called ESM, AlphaFold-Multimer, and Rosetta to refine nanobodies; Paper2Agent's AlphaGenome tools outperformed general agents, showing that packaging matters.

3-05e2.text: Text: each cell as a list of its top genes.

3-06e1.text: BioReason: on pathway questions the LLM alone reached 90% and the encoder made little difference; on variant classification it reached 49%, rising to 80% with Evo 2 vs. 61% with Nucleotide Transformer.

5.1-03e1.text: Systems feeding FM embeddings into an LLM rarely report controls separating encoder and LLM contributions; applied to six systems, BioReason and BioReason-Pro were as accurate with shuffled biological inputs as with intact ones.

4-01e1.text: Why "extinct": the vocabulary must be inferred, no living speaker can confirm the grammar, and the only surviving texts are the measurements assays happened to record.

4-01e2.text: Why LLM boundaries are hidden: modern language is densely represented in their training data.

4.2-01e3.text: Each answer rests on comparing model outputs with independent data or on laboratory tests of designs.

4.1-03e1.text: ChromBPNet (CNN): ~2 kb at single-base resolution, suited to motifs and variants within them. Enformer (adds attention): regulatory elements ~100 kb away. HyenaDNA: one million nucleotides.

4.1-05e3.text: How a benchmark is split and which simple baselines it includes decides which weaknesses can be seen.

4.3-04e2.text: For genetic perturbation responses, simple linear models and even the average of the training data match or outperform FMs.
4.3-04e2.finding: Observed states rarely predict the effect of an intervention beyond simple baselines

4.3-04e3.text: Single-cell: Geneformer and scGPT embeddings did not outperform simple baselines without fine-tuning; L1-regularized logistic regression rivaled scBERT; parameter-free representations match single-cell FMs; GenePT suggests part of what these models learn is already recorded in text.
4.3-04e3.finding: Observed states rarely predict the effect of an intervention beyond simple baselines

4.3-04e4.text: Similar results for mutation-dense protein design and for multi-omics integration (no uniform advantage across 23 methods).
4.3-04e4.finding: Observed states rarely predict the effect of an intervention beyond simple baselines

4.3-05e1.text: DNA language models are spread across competing benchmarks, with inconsistent gains over lightweight supervised models.
4.3-05e1.finding: Tests sometimes do not measure what they claim

4.3-06e3.text: Most of 21 pretrained RNA language models did not outperform one-hot encoding for secondary-structure prediction once closely related sequences were removed from the test set.

4.3-02e1.text: Protein language model likelihoods partly reflect how often related sequences were sampled across the tree of life rather than fitness alone.
4.3-02e1.finding: Models capture both biology and the history of sampling

4.3-02e2.text: Gene-function annotation can become circular: curated databases shaped both LLM-based annotators' training and the benchmark labels; they perform worse on orphan genes and non-model organisms.
4.3-02e2.finding: Models capture both biology and the history of sampling

4.3-05e2.text: Common perturbation metrics are dominated by systematic expression differences unrelated to the specific perturbation, so a model can score well by predicting an average response.
4.3-05e2.finding: Tests sometimes do not measure what they claim

4.3-05e3.text: Conversely, when metrics are calibrated against an uninformative mean baseline and a positive control, several deep-learning perturbation models do outperform simple baselines; part of the reported parity reflects the metric, not the model.
4.3-05e3.finding: Tests sometimes do not measure what they claim

4.3-03e2.text: Larger protein language models do not consistently improve zero-shot fitness prediction; downstream tasks often reuse features learned early in pretraining.
4.3-03e2.finding: One-mutation effects are often missed, and scale has not closed the gap

5.2-02e1.finding: One-mutation effects are often missed, and scale has not closed the gap

5.2-03e1.finding: One-mutation effects are often missed, and scale has not closed the gap

5.3-02e1.text: Historical parallel: Darwin's cataloguing of species.

5.3-02e2.text: Claims framed in engineering-stage language, such as "de novo design," should be read with this stage in mind.

6.2-01e1.text: Tool descriptions state what a tool does but seldom where it fails; a variant score from a model trained without population data looks as authoritative as a well-supported result.

6.2-02e1.text: Contents of a boundary statement, organized by the five design elements: species, assays, and conditions in the training data; context length and tokenization; training objective; benchmarks used, including comparisons with simple baselines; and the post-analysis methods under which the reported results hold.

6.2-03e1.text: Just as GeneAgent checks its claims against curated databases, an agent could confirm a query lies within a model's training and evaluation domain before relying on its output.

6.2-04e1.text: Agents that plan experiments + FMs that propose candidates + self-driving labs = closed loops that target boundary regions directly.

6.3-02e1.text: Embedded-scientist programs, reciprocal laboratory placements, fellowships, and professional community-management roles offer deeper cross-disciplinary exposure than short courses.

6.3-01e1.text: UniProt and the PDB became trusted infrastructure; open-source ecosystems made models widely reusable; blind assessments such as CASP and CAGI established credible measures of progress.

6.3-03e1.text: Existing precedent for model exchange: Kipoi repository.
